title: The Realms of Water

overview.intro: Water is the only substance that occurs naturally on the Earth as solid, liquid and gas, and it moves continuously between the oceans, the land and the atmosphere. This hydrological cycle links every part of the planet: evaporation supplies the atmosphere, precipitation returns it to the surface, and runoff and groundwater bring it back to the sea. This unit covers the properties that make water unusual, the processes of the hydrological cycle, the temperature and salinity structure of the oceans, and the currents and waves that move ocean water.

facts.label: Distribution
facts.value: About 97% of Earth’s water is in the oceans, about 2% is frozen in ice caps and glaciers, and under 1% is liquid freshwater available in rivers, lakes and groundwater.

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff and storage, driven by solar energy and gravity.

facts.label: Properties
facts.value: High specific heat, high latent heat of vaporisation, maximum density at 4°C and expansion on freezing.

facts.label: Currents
facts.value: Surface currents driven by prevailing winds; deep currents driven by differences in temperature and salinity.

learningOutcomes: Describe the hydrological cycle and its components.
Explain the properties of water that make it important for climate.
Describe the temperature and salinity structure of the oceans.
Explain the formation and effects of ocean currents.
Describe waves, tides and the movement of ocean water.

blocks.text: The hydrological cycle is the continuous movement of water between the ocean, the atmosphere and the land, powered by solar energy which drives evaporation and by gravity which returns water to the sea. Water evaporates from the ocean surface and from land and water bodies, and plants add transpiration to the atmosphere. In the air it cools and condenses around nuclei into clouds, and it returns as precipitation, falling as rain, snow or hail. Some precipitation runs off the surface into streams and rivers, some infiltrates the soil to recharge groundwater, and some is stored in snow, ice, soil moisture, lakes and glaciers before continuing.

items: The ocean is the largest store and the principal source of evaporation.
Soil moisture is the short-term reservoir on which plants depend.
Groundwater moves slowly and can discharge springs and wells for years.
Glaciers store water for centuries, delaying its return to the sea.
Human use of rivers and aquifers changes the local cycle substantially.

learn.title: Properties of water that matter for the Earth system

blocks.text: Water has four properties with consequences far beyond drinking. Its specific heat is high, so a given quantity absorbs much energy before warming, which makes the ocean a great regulator of climate. Its latent heat of vaporisation is large, so evaporation removes enormous heat from a surface and returns it when the vapour condenses, which is how tropical storms are powered. It expands slightly on freezing rather than contracting, which makes ice float, insulating the water below and allowing life to survive winter. And its maximum density occurs at about 4 degrees Celsius, so cold water sinks below both warmer and freezing water, driving vertical mixing in lakes and oceans.

learn.title: Temperature, salinity and the structure of ocean water

blocks.text: Sea temperature falls with latitude because the angle and duration of insolation differ, and it falls with depth because little radiation penetrates beyond the first few hundred metres. The vertical change is not uniform: a thermocline separates the warm surface water from the cold deep water, and it acts as a barrier to mixing. Salinity varies with the balance of evaporation and precipitation, with river input and with ice formation, and it is highest in enclosed basins with high evaporation such as the Red Sea and the Mediterranean, and lowest where rivers dilute the sea such as the Baltic.

Temperature and salinity together determine density, and density determines where water sinks. Surface water that becomes cold and salty grows dense and sinks, forming deep water that creeps along the ocean floor, while warmer water returns at the surface. This thermohaline circulation exchanges water between basins over centuries and is a major regulator of global climate.

blocks.caption: Factors governing ocean salinity
rows: High evaporation in subtropical latitudes
Heavy rainfall near the equator
Formation of sea ice, which rejects salt
River discharge into a sea
Restricted basins with little exchange
Melting of sea ice
Low cloud cover and dry winds
Strong vertical mixing of the water column

blocks.text: Ocean currents are continuous, directed movements of water, and surface currents are driven chiefly by the prevailing winds, deflected by the rotation of the Earth and shaped by the form of the land. Warm currents move from lower to higher latitudes and raise the temperature and humidity of the coasts they pass, while cold currents move from higher to lower latitudes and tend to cool and dry the adjacent land. The great gyres, the large loops formed where currents are turned back by continental margins, circulate in opposite directions in the two hemispheres because of the Coriolis deflection.

Waves are oscillations of the water surface in which energy travels while the water particles move in circles. As a wave enters shallow water the base drags on the seabed, the wave slows, steepens and breaks, which is how surf is produced. Tides are the periodic rise and fall of sea level caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and, to a lesser extent, the sun. When the two align at new and full moon the effects add to give spring tides, and when they act at right angles at the quarter moons the effects partially cancel to give neap tides.

blocks.caption: Tides and their causes

items: Warm currents moderate the climate of western coasts at high latitude.
Cold currents support rich fisheries by bringing nutrient-rich water to the surface.
Upwelling occurs where wind pushes surface water away and deep water rises to replace it.
Fog forms where a cold current meets warm moist air above it.
The Coriolis effect makes currents in the northern hemisphere circulate clockwise.

keyPoints: The hydrological cycle moves water between ocean, atmosphere and land, driven by solar energy and gravity.
About 97 per cent of Earth’s water is in the oceans and less than 1 per cent is accessible liquid freshwater.
Water has a high specific heat, which moderates coastal climate.
Water has a high latent heat of vaporisation, which powers storms when vapour condenses.
Water is densest at 4 degrees Celsius and expands when it freezes, so ice floats.
Sea temperature falls with latitude and with depth, with a thermocline separating warm and cold water.
Salinity rises with evaporation and ice formation and falls with rainfall and river input.
Density differences from temperature and salinity drive thermohaline circulation.
Surface currents are driven by winds; deep currents by density differences.
Tides result from lunar and solar gravity, giving spring tides at new and full moon and neaps at the quarter moons.
examFocus: Cycle diagrams should be labelled and show a closed loop, since a one-way arrow loses marks.
Property questions earn marks by pairing each property with its real-world consequence.
Tide answers must state why spring and neap tides differ, which lies in the alignment of sun and moon.

questions.prompt: The process by which water returns from the atmosphere to the surface is:
questions.explanation: Precipitation returns water as rain, snow or hail, closing the loop between atmosphere and surface.

options: Ice is less dense than water
Water reaches its maximum density at 4°C and expands when it freezes
Salt raises the density of water
The ice is warmed from below
questions.answer: Water reaches its maximum density at 4°C and expands when it freezes
questions.explanation: Water is densest at 4 degrees and expands as it cools further and freezes, making ice the lighter of the two.

options: At the first and third quarter moon
When the sun and moon are aligned at new and full moon
When a cold current meets a warm one
questions.answer: When the sun and moon are aligned at new and full moon
questions.explanation: Alignment of the solar and lunar tidal pulls gives the greatest range of high and low water.

questions.prompt: A coastal desert cooled by mist but receiving almost no rain is best explained by:
options: A cold current cooling the air and suppressing rainfall
questions.answer: A cold current cooling the air and suppressing rainfall
questions.explanation: Cold currents cool and stabilise the lower air, inhibiting the convection needed for rain, while fog forms as moist air passes over the cold surface.

questions.prompt: The continuous movement of water between the ocean, atmosphere and land is called the hydrological __________ .
questions.explanation: It is powered by solar energy for evaporation and by gravity for the return flow to the sea.

questions.prompt: The layer in the ocean where temperature falls rapidly with depth is called the __________ .
questions.explanation: It separates warm surface water from cold deep water and acts as a barrier to vertical mixing.

questions.prompt: State four processes of the hydrological cycle with their direction of movement.
questions.answer: Four processes are: evaporation, in which liquid water on the surface becomes water vapour in the atmosphere; condensation, in which vapour cools into droplets and forms cloud; precipitation, in which water falls from cloud to the surface as rain, snow or hail; and infiltration, in which surface water moves downward into soil and rock. Transpiration from plant leaves and runoff returning to rivers are also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each process needs its direction stated, since naming a process without its movement does not show understanding.

questions.prompt: Explain four factors that affect the salinity of sea water.
questions.answer: Four factors are: evaporation, which concentrates salt and raises salinity, so subtropical seas are saltiest; precipitation, which dilutes the surface water, so equatorial regions are less saline; river discharge, which adds freshwater and lowers salinity, as in the Baltic Sea; and the formation of sea ice, which rejects salt into the surrounding water and raises salinity. Melting ice has the opposite effect, lowering salinity.
questions.explanation: Each factor needs the direction of its effect and an illustration, since the direction is what carries the marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the hydrological cycle and explain why it is important.
questions.answer: The hydrological cycle is the continuous movement of water among the ocean, the atmosphere and the land, powered by solar energy and returned by gravity. Water evaporates from the ocean surface and from land and lakes, while plants add transpiration, and together they supply the atmosphere with moisture. In the air the vapour cools and condenses around nuclei into clouds and returns as precipitation. Some of that water runs off the surface into streams and rivers, some infiltrates the soil to recharge groundwater, and some is stored in snow, ice, soil moisture and lakes before moving on, so that water eventually reaches the ocean and the cycle begins again. Its importance is that it redistributes both water and energy: latent heat carried in vapour and released in condensation moves heat from the tropics toward higher latitudes, groundwater storage supplies rivers and wells during dry periods, and the storage in ice delays the return of water by years. The cycle is also the mechanism by which freshwater is renewed, which is what makes continuous human settlement possible.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the closed loop described process by process and at least two reasons for its importance.

questions.prompt: Explain why the western coast of a continent near 50 degrees north has a mild, wet climate while the eastern coast near the same latitude has a cold, dry one, using ocean currents.
questions.answer: The difference lies in the currents that each coast meets, which is set by the direction of the ocean gyre. On the western coast, at about 50 degrees north, the current arriving from lower latitudes is a warm current, which transfers heat to the air above it, raises its temperature and humidity, and gives mild winters with considerable cloud and rain. On the eastern coast at the same latitude, the gyre returns cold water from higher latitudes, so the current is a cold one: it cools the air in contact with it, stabilises the lower atmosphere by chilling it from below, and suppresses the convection needed for rainfall, giving cool summers and dry conditions. Warm currents therefore moderate western coasts while cold currents cool and dry eastern ones, which is why western Europe enjoys a mild maritime climate at latitudes that are far colder on the eastern side of continents. The Coriolis deflection explains the direction of the gyre that produces this pairing, with clockwise circulation in the northern hemisphere carrying warm water poleward on the western side of the basin.
questions.explanation: The answer is marked on naming the current type at each coast and then tracing the effect through heating, humidity and stability rather than simply asserting a climatic difference.
